interactiveFlow.title: The Request and Response cycle
interactiveFlow.subtitle: Move step by step and follow how the message leaves the client, passes through the API, and returns ready for the interface.
interactiveFlow.requestLaneLead: The question is entering the system.
interactiveFlow.responseLaneLead: The answer is returning to the interface.
interactiveFlow.requestLaneDescription: First the client builds the intent, chooses the endpoint, and hands the message to the API to validate and process it.
interactiveFlow.responseLaneDescription: After processing, the server builds the HTTP response and the interface translates the technical result into something visual for the user.

rrCycle.title: The technical journey from Request to Response
rrCycle.subtitle: Follow the full path of the message: intent on the client, validation in the API, processing on the server, and the return to the interface.

clientClick.title: The client decides to act
clientClick.desc: Everything starts when the {{Client}} needs something: open a screen, submit a form, or refresh a panel. Without that initiative, nothing happens in the classic {{HTTP}} model.
clientClick.debug: First ask: who triggered the action and in what context?
clientClick.hint: There is no error yet here. This step only shows that the flow always starts on the user side, never with the {{Server}} pushing data on its own.

requestAssembled.title: The Request is assembled
requestAssembled.desc: The {{Client}} organizes the {{Request}} with an {{HTTP Method}}, an {{Endpoint}}, {{Headers}}, and maybe a {{Body}}. This package travels with explicit intent.
requestAssembled.debug: Check method, path, headers, and payload before blaming the API.
requestAssembled.hint: When assembly goes wrong, common problems usually appear as {{400 Bad Request}}, {{401 Unauthorized}}, or {{415 Unsupported Media Type}}.

apiValidation.title: The API performs triage
apiValidation.desc: The {{API}} receives the packet and decides whether it deserves to enter. Here it validates format, authentication, route, and contract before triggering business logic.
apiValidation.debug: If it failed early, the clue usually lives in the {{Headers}}, the {{Path}}, or the {{Body}} type.
apiValidation.hint: Think of the {{API}} as a digital gatekeeper: it blocks malformed requests before spending server processing power.

serverProcessing.title: The server processes the rule
serverProcessing.desc: After triage, the {{Server}} executes the application logic. This is where it queries data, calculates prices, applies permissions, and decides the outcome.
serverProcessing.debug: If the contract was correct and it still broke, start investigating business logic or internal failure.
serverProcessing.hint: Not every server-side issue becomes {{500 Internal Server Error}}. Sometimes the logic works and deliberately returns {{404 Not Found}} or another status.

responseBuilt.title: The Response is built
responseBuilt.desc: Once the decision is made, the system assembles the {{Response}}: a {{Status Code}}, output {{Headers}}, and possibly a {{Body}} with data or an error message.
responseBuilt.debug: The first summary of the story always lives in the {{Status Code}}.
responseBuilt.hint: The {{Response}} is not cosmetic detail. It is the final contract telling whether the operation created, found, rejected, or broke something.

interfaceRendered.title: The interface translates the result
interfaceRendered.desc: The {{Interface}} reads the {{Response}} and converts technical data into a human-facing screen: list, alert, validation error, or success confirmation.
interfaceRendered.packet: Screen render with success or error
interfaceRendered.debug: Good frontend code does not ignore the error body; it interprets the full {{Response}}.
interfaceRendered.hint: When the UI shows something strange, confirm whether the bug is in the {{Interface}} rendering or whether it was born earlier inside the {{Response}} itself.

rrAnatomy.title: Request on one side, Response on the other
rrAnatomy.subtitle: Click each block and see which part of the conversation belongs to sending the request and which belongs to the server's return.

method.title: Request method
method.desc: The {{HTTP Method}} is the verb of the conversation. It tells whether the {{Client}} wants to fetch, create, update, or remove something.
method.debug: If the method is wrong, the API may answer with {{400 Bad Request}} or reject the expected action semantically.

path.title: Path and Endpoint
path.desc: The {{Path}} points to the right resource inside the {{Endpoint}}. It tells where the {{Request}} should land.
path.debug: A wrong path often explains {{404 Not Found}} without any real server drama.

requestHeaders.title: Request headers
requestHeaders.desc: The {{Request}} {{Headers}} carry metadata: identity, payload format, preferred language, and other invisible clues.
requestHeaders.debug: Authentication and format errors almost always start here.

requestBody.title: Request body
requestBody.desc: The {{Body}} carries the useful load. In write operations, the {{Payload}} usually travels here as {{JSON}}.
requestBody.debug: If the payload structure is wrong, the server may reject the operation before business logic even runs.

status.title: Response status
status.desc: The {{Status Code}} is the executive summary of the answer. It quickly says whether things worked, something was missing, or an internal failure happened.
status.debug: Learn to read the number before speculating: it cuts half the diagnosis.

responseHeaders.title: Response headers
responseHeaders.desc: The {{Response}} {{Headers}} return technical context: content type, location of the created resource, and useful tracing identifiers.
responseHeaders.debug: When the body is not enough, output headers often reveal contract, cache, or traceability details.

responseBody.title: Response body
responseBody.desc: The {{Response}} {{Body}} delivers data, messages, or error details. It is the material the {{Interface}} will interpret.
responseBody.debug: Ignoring the response body means throwing away the explanation the API just gave you.

rrExamples.title: Three scenarios to lock the cycle in
rrExamples.subtitle: See how behavior changes when the goal is only to read data, create a new resource, or ask for something that does not exist.

get.title: Simple data read
get.desc: A read {{Request}} usually does not need a {{Body}}. The focus is on the {{Path}} and the {{Headers}}.
get.takeaway: When you only want to query, the cycle is leaner: a read {{HTTP Method}}, no {{Payload}}, and a success {{Status Code}} coming back.

post.title: Creation with payload
post.desc: A write operation needs more context: filled {{Body}}, correct contract, and a coherent creation response.
post.request:
POST /api/orders HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer demo-token
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "productId": 42,
  "quantity": 1
}
post.takeaway: Here the full cycle is visible: intent in the {{HTTP Method}}, data in the {{Body}}, and confirmation through {{201 Created}}.

notFound.title: Requesting a missing resource
notFound.desc: Not every error means the system is down. Sometimes the {{Request}} arrived correctly, but the requested resource simply does not exist.
notFound.takeaway: The {{404 Not Found}} teaches you to separate missing route or missing resource from a true {{500 Internal Server Error}}.

rrMistakes.title: Four interpretation mistakes that slow down debugging
rrMistakes.subtitle: These mistakes make people look at the wrong part of the cycle and waste time fixing what is not actually broken.

serverDown.title: Treating 404 like server outage
serverDown.wrong: Receiving {{404 Not Found}} does not automatically mean the {{Server}} is down. Often the cycle worked, but the {{Path}} or requested resource does not exist.
serverDown.correction: Read {{404 Not Found}} as a clue about address or missing resource. Save {{500 Internal Server Error}} for true internal failures.

getBody.title: Assuming GET depends on a body
getBody.wrong: Forcing a {{Body}} into every {{Request}} blurs the mental model. In simple reads, the common pattern is {{GET}} without {{Payload}}.
getBody.correction: Use the {{Body}} when the intent truly requires sending data. For queries, prefer {{Path}}, query string, and {{Headers}}.

ignoreResponse.title: Looking only at the number and ignoring the body
ignoreResponse.wrong: Reading only the {{Status Code}} and ignoring the {{Body}} of the {{Response}} makes you miss message, context, and error details.
ignoreResponse.correction: The number summarizes; the body explains. Mature debugging reads the full {{Response}}.

uiVsApi.title: Blaming the API for every strange screen
uiVsApi.wrong: If the {{Interface}} renders something incorrectly, that does not prove the {{API}} answered incorrectly. The problem may be in frontend data transformation.
uiVsApi.correction: Compare the real {{Response}} with what the {{Interface}} displayed. That is how you separate contract bugs from rendering bugs.
